result:
All three solutions give the same final answer, $\binom{N+1}{3}=\frac{(N-1)N(N+1)}{6}$, so they stand or fall together.

The count of triples $2\le a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le N$ is correct. The open question is whether distinct triples give non-isomorphic surfaces. Solution 1 gives the most concrete argument: isomorphic varieties are diffeomorphic, and the Milnor number together with the Brieskorn link (its Seifert invariants and $H_1$) separates the triples. Its case analysis is only sketched, and I did not verify it. Solution 2 asserts the isomorphism claim without proof. Solution 3 relies on unproven claims about the class group and the fundamental group, though its small checks are correct.

I could not confirm from memory a published theorem establishing that all these surfaces are pairwise non-isomorphic, so I cannot rule out coincidences that would lower the count. I therefore lean toward the common answer, with Solution 1 as the best-supported of the three.

CHOICE: 1
